Since they were not, God imposed them upon them on the Day of Resurrection as a form of punishment.

As for the second way, namely that they all occur in this world: it is said that they are the people of the monasteries from among the Jews, Christians, idol-worshippers and Magians. The meaning is that they were humbled before God, laboured and grew exhausted in their deeds, through continual fasting and wearisome night prayer. This is because, having believed things about God that are not fitting for Him, it is as though they obeyed an essence described by the attributes they imagined. In reality, they did not worship God, but worshipped that imagined thing which has no existence. Therefore that worship does not benefit them at all.

As for the third way, namely that some of these attributes occur in the Hereafter and some in this world, there are several interpretations:

One of them: they will be humbled in the Hereafter, although in this world they were labouring and exhausted. The meaning is that they did not benefit from their labour and exhaustion in this world. It is not impossible to describe them with some attributes of the Hereafter, then mention some attributes of this world, and then mention the Hereafter again, when the meaning in that is understood. It is as though He, exalted is He, said: faces on the Day of Resurrection will be humbled, because in this world they were labouring and exhausted in other than obedience to God. Therefore they will then burn in a scorching Fire in the Hereafter.

The second: they will be humbled and labouring in this world, but exhausted in the Hereafter. Their humility in this world is their fear, which prompted them to turn away from the pleasures and good things of this world. Their labour is their prayer and fasting. Their exhaustion in the Hereafter is their suffering the punishment, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and there will appear to them from God what they had not reckoned﴾ [al-Zumar: 47]. It was also read as "labouring, exhausted" with a stressed (accusative) form. Know that, after describing them with these three attributes, He, exalted is He, then explained the nature of their dwelling, their drink and their food. We seek refuge in God from them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 88, verse 5–6:

As for their drink, the words of Allah the Exalted are: ﴿They will be given to drink from a boiling spring﴾. The word āniyah (boiling, at its utmost heat) is derived from the root ana, which means that its heat has reached its limit, from al-iyna' in the sense of delay. In a hadith: "A man delayed attending the Friday prayer, then he stepped over the necks of the people, so the Prophet ﷺ said to him: 'You have delayed and you have harmed.'" A parallel to this verse is His words: ﴿They will go around between it and a scalding hot water (ḥamīm āniy)﴾ [al-Rahman: 44]. The exegetes said: its heat has reached such a degree that if a single drop of it fell upon the mountains of the world, they would melt.

As for their food, the words of Allah the Exalted are: ﴿They will have no food except from ḍarī' (a thorny plant)﴾. The scholars differed over what ḍarī' is, and they gave several opinions:

First: al-Hasan said: "I do not know what ḍarī' is, and I have not heard anything about it from the Companions."

Second: It is also narrated from al-Hasan that he said: ḍarī' is in the sense of muḍri' (causing distress), like alīm (painful) and samī' (hearing) and badī' (originating) in the sense of mu'lim (causing pain), musmi' (causing to hear) and mubdi' (originating). Its meaning is: "except from food that makes them humble and submissive when they eat it, because of its roughness, bitterness and heat."

Third: ḍarī' is what has dried of al-shibriq, which is a kind of thorn that camels graze upon while it is moist; when it dries, they avoid it, and it is a deadly poison. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

It grazed on the lush shibriq until it withered and became ḍarī', and the camels that are not pregnant (nuḥuṣ) turned away from it.

Nuḥuṣ is the plural of nāḥiṣ, which is a she-camel that does not conceive. This is the view of most exegetes and most lexicographers.

Fourth: al-Khalil said in his book: "ḍarī' is also said of the membrane that lies over the bone beneath the flesh." So it seems that Allah described it as having little substance, and therefore it neither fattens nor relieves hunger.

Fifth: Abu al-Jawza' said: "ḍarī' is al-salā (the membrane covering the bones)." Close to this is what is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that it is a thorny tree. Then Abu al-Jawza' said: "How can one grow fat who eats thorns!" And in a report: "ḍarī' is something found in the Fire, resembling thorns, more bitter than aloes, more foul-smelling than carrion, and hotter than the Fire itself."

Al-Qaffal said: The purpose of mentioning this drink and this food is to show the extreme of their humiliation. For when these people remained for that long period in those chains and shackles, thirsty and hungry, and then they were thrown into the Fire, they saw in it water and some vegetation. Those people longed to quench their thirst and hunger, but they found the water to be boiling, which does not quench but scalds, and they found the vegetation to be something that does not satisfy nor relieve hunger. So they despaired, and their hopes of removing their hunger and thirst were cut off, as He said: ﴿And if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten metal﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. He made clear that this state does not cease or end. We seek refuge in Allah from it.

First question: Allah said in surah al-Haqqah: ﴿So there is no friend for him here today, nor any food except from ghislin (pus)﴾ [al-Haqqah: 35–36]. And here He said: ﴿They will have no food except from ḍarī'﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6]. And ḍarī' is other than ghislin.

The answer is in two ways:

First: The Fire has levels. Among the people of the Fire there are those whose food is zaqqum, and among them are those whose food is ghislin, and among them are those whose food is ḍarī', and among them are those whose drink is ḥamīm, and among them are those whose drink is ṣadīd. "For each gate of them there is an allotted portion."

Second: It is possible that ghislin is from ḍarī', and that is like saying: "I have no food except from the sheep," and then saying: "I have no food except from milk," with no contradiction, since milk comes from the sheep.

The answer is in two ways:

First: The meaning is not that ḍarī' is a plant in the Fire that they eat; rather, it is a kind similar to it, i.e., they sustain themselves on something that does not satisfy them, or they are punished with hunger, just as one who has ḍarī' as his food is punished.

Second: Why should it not be said that plant life exists in the Fire? Since the survival of the human body, being flesh and blood, in the Fire forever and ever is not considered far-fetched, the same applies here. The same is true of the chains of the Fire, its shackles, its scorpions and its serpents.

Here there are some questions:

First question: Allah said in surah al-Haqqah: ﴿So there is no friend for him here today, nor any food except from ghislin (pus)﴾ [al-Haqqah: 35–36]. And here He said: ﴿They will have no food except from ḍarī'﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6]. And ḍarī' is other than ghislin.

The answer is in two ways:

First: The Fire has levels. The answer is in two ways:

First: The meaning is not that ḍarī' is a plant in the Fire that they eat; rather, it is a kind similar to it, i.e., they sustain themselves on something that does not satisfy them, or they are punished with hunger, just as one who has ḍarī' as his food is punished.

The second [aspect concerns] their inner state, which is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Pleased with their striving﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

The first: They will praise their striving and their effort in working for God, because of the good end they attained through it. [This is] like a man who does a deed and is rewarded for it with goodness, and who sees from it a praiseworthy outcome, so he says: "How excellent is what I did, and indeed I was granted success in what is right in what I accomplished," and so he commends his own deed and is pleased with it.

The second: The meaning is that they will be pleased with the reward of their striving in the world when they witness that reward. This is the more preferable [interpretation], since the meaning is that the great reward they witness reaches the degree of satisfaction, so that they do not desire more than it. As for the description of the abode of reward, know that God, Exalted is He, described it with seven qualities:

[Page 141]

The first of them is His saying: ﴿In a lofty Garden﴾. It may be that the intended meaning is loftiness in place, and it may be that the intended meaning is loftiness in rank, nobility and excellence. As for loftiness in place, that is because Paradise has levels, some of which are higher than others. ʿAtāʾ said: "The [distance of] a level is like what is between the heaven and the earth."

The second: His saying: ﴿Wherein they hear no idle talk﴾. Concerning this there are two questions:

The first question: Regarding His saying "lā tasmaʿu" (they do not hear), there are three readings:

The first: ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read it with the letter tāʾ, in the second person address ("you do not hear"), with "lāghiyatan" in the accusative. The one addressed by this address may be the Prophet ﷺ, or it may be that the meaning is "you [O addressee] do not hear therein idle talk." This implies hearing in address, like His saying: ﴿And when you look there, you see [bliss]﴾ [al-Insān: 20] and His saying: ﴿When you see them, you think them﴾ [al-Insān: 19]. It is also possible that this tāʾ refers to faces, and the meaning is: the faces do not hear therein idle talk.

The second: Nāfiʿ read it with a tāʾ with a dot above, marfūʿah (in the nominative), in the feminine form, "lāghiyatun" in the nominative.

The third: Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read "lā yusmaʿu" with a yāʾ with a dot below, ḍammah (vowelled with a ḍammah), in the masculine form, "lāghiyatun" in the nominative. This is permissible for two reasons:

The first: that this type of feminine noun, when its verb precedes it and there is a separation between the verb and the noun, the masculine form is acceptable. The poet said:

"If a woman deceives you among them, one [woman] after me and after you in this world, then indeed she is deceived."

The second: that the intended meaning of "lāghiyah" is idle talk (laghw), so the feminine form is according to the wording and the masculine form according to the meaning.

The second question: Concerning His saying ﴿lāghiyatan﴾, the lexicographers have three opinions:

The first: It is said: "laghā yalghū laghwan wa lāghiyatan," so "al-lāghiyah" and "al-laghw" are one and the same thing. This opinion is reinforced by the saying of the Glorified: ﴿They do not hear therein any idle talk [laghw]﴾ [al-Wāqiʿah: 25].

The third: al-Akhfash said: "lāghiyatan" means a word possessing idle talk, just as you say "fāris" and "dāriʿ" for the owner of the horse and the armour.

As for the exegetes, they have several opinions:

The first: Paradise is free of idle talk, because it is the abode of the neighbours of God, Exalted is He, and they attained it through seriousness and truth, not through idle talk and falsehood. The fifth: al-Qāḍī said: idle talk is that which has no benefit in it. God, Exalted is He, negated this from them, and included in this, by way of greater precedence, whatever would harm the one who hears it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 88, verse 17–19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, decreed the coming of the Day of Resurrection, and divided the people of the Resurrection into two groups, the wretched and the blessed, and described the conditions of both groups, and it was known that there is no way to establish that except through establishing the Wise Creator (al-Sani' al-Hakim), He therefore followed that with mention of this proof, saying: ﴿Do they not look at the camels﴾. The way of inferring from it the soundness of the return (al-ma'ad) is that it indicates the existence of the Wise Creator, and once that is established, the affirmation of the soundness of the return is established.

As for the first point: bodies are equal in corporeality, so the specification of each one of them with the attribute by which it is distinguished from the other must have a specifier (mukhassis) and a capable originator (ijad qadir). And since we see these bodies created in a manner of perfection and precision, we know that this Creator is knowing. And since we know that this Creator must be different from His creation in the attribute of need, contingency and possibility, we know that He is self-sufficient (ghani). This indicates that the world has a Creator who is capable, knowing and self-sufficient, and so He must be in the utmost wisdom. Furthermore, we see that people are in need of one another, for a single person cannot manage the affairs of himself alone; rather there must be a town in which each of its inhabitants is occupied with another task, so that from the whole of them the benefit of each one of them is organized. That organization is not good except with obligation (taklif) that includes promise and threat, and that is not achieved except through resurrection, the Day of Judgment, and the creation of Paradise and Hell. Thus it is established that establishing the proof of the Wise Creator necessitates affirming the soundness of resurrection and the Day of Judgment. For this reason Allah mentioned the proof of Tawhid at the end of this surah. If it is said: What affinity is there between the camels, the sky, the mountains and the earth? And why did He begin with mention of the camels?

We say: There are two aspects to this.

The first: all created things are equal in this proof, and mentioning all of them is not possible because of their multitude; and whichever one of them is mentioned without the others, this question would apply. So it is necessary to rule that this question falls away in all cases. Also, perhaps the wisdom in mentioning these things that are not analogous is to alert to the fact that this mode of inference is not specific to one kind rather than another, but is general across all, as in His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra' 44]. Had He mentioned other than these, the matter would not be so; therefore Allah, exalted is He, mentioned matters that are not analogous, rather very distant from one another, as an alert that all the heavenly and earthly bodies, small and large, beautiful and ugly, are equal in indicating the Wise Creator. This is a good and reasonable aspect, and upon it reliance is placed.

The second aspect: that we explain what is in each one of these things of benefits and properties that indicate the need for a Creator who governs, then we explain how some of them are analogous to others.

As for the first point: we say: the camel has properties, among them that Allah, exalted is He, made the animal that is kept into various kinds: sometimes it is kept to be eaten for its meat, sometimes for its milk to be drunk, sometimes to carry a person on journeys, sometimes to transport a person's goods from one town to another, and sometimes to have adornment and beauty from it. All these benefits are gathered in the camel, and Allah, mighty and majestic, has made this clear by His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We created for them, of what Our hands have made, livestock, so that they are its owners? And We subjected them to them, so some of them are their mounts, and of them they eat﴾ [Ya-Sin 71-72], and He said: ﴿And the livestock, He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and of them you eat. And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home in the evening and when you send them out to pasture. And they carry your loads to a land you could not reach except with great hardship﴾ [al-Nahl 5-7]. And indeed none of the rest of the animals gathers these qualities in itself, so the gathering of these qualities in it is among the wonders.

Second: in each one of these qualities it is superior to the animal in which only that one quality is found. For if it is made a milker, it gives drink and quenches much; if it is made an eater (for food), it feeds and satisfies much; if it is made a mount, it is possible to cover with it distances so long that cannot be covered with another animal. That is because of what is composed in it of the strength to bear persistence in travel, patience with thirst, and contentment with fodder with what no other animal is content with. And if it is made a carrier, it is employed in carrying heavy loads which no other animal can bear alone. Among them also is that this animal was the greatest of animals in impact upon the hearts of the Arabs; for this reason they made the blood-money (diyah) for killing a person in camels, and when one of their kings wished to show great generosity to a poet who had come to him from a distant place, he gave him a hundred camels, because the eye's being filled with it is more intense than its being filled with anything else. For this reason Allah said: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home in the evening and when you send them out to pasture﴾ [al-Nahl 6]. Among them also: I was once with a group in a desert, and we lost the way, and they sent a camel ahead and followed it, and that camel kept turning from hill to hill and from side to side, and all of them followed it until it reached the road after a long time. We marvelled at the power of imagination in that animal: how the image of those turnings was preserved in its imagination after a single occurrence, to the point that what a group of intelligent people failed to find, that animal found. Among them also: that it, while being in the utmost strength for work, is distinct from others in its submission and obedience even to the weakest of animals, such as a small child; and it is also distinct from others in that it is loaded while it is kneeling and then it rises. These many attributes found in it oblige the intelligent person to look at its creation and composition and to infer from that the existence of the Wise Creator, glory be to Him. Moreover, the Arabs are among the people most knowledgeable of the conditions of camels in their health and sickness, their benefits and harms; therefore, for these reasons it was fitting from the Wise, exalted is He, to command reflection upon its creation.

These many attributes found in it oblige the intelligent person to look at its creation and composition and to infer from that the existence of the Wise Creator, glory be to Him. Moreover, the Arabs are among the people most knowledgeable of the conditions of camels in their health and sickness, their benefits and harms; therefore, for these reasons it was fitting from the Wise, exalted is He, to command reflection upon its creation.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And at the sky, how it was raised﴾, meaning raised to a great height, without support and without pillars.

﴿And at the mountains, how they were set firm﴾, set in a firm manner, so they are steadfast, not leaning and not moving.

Some people have used this to argue that the earth is not a sphere, but this is weak, because if a sphere is extremely large, every part of it appears like a flat surface. ʿAlī, peace be upon him, read: "how I created, raised, set firm and spread out," with the verb in the first person active and the ta' of the pronoun, and the implied meaning is "I did it," so the object was omitted.

The second topic: explaining the connection between these things. Know that some people interpreted the camels (al-ibil) as clouds. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Perhaps he did not mean that al-ibil is among the names of clouds, like al-ghamam, al-muzn, al-rabab, al-ghaym and al-ghayn and others, but rather he saw clouds being compared to camels in much of their poetry, so he permitted that clouds be meant by it by way of simile and metaphor." The first: the Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and they traveled a great deal, because their town was a land free of cultivation, and their journeys were for the most part on camels. They often journeyed on them through deserts and wastelands, feeling lonely and isolated from people. It is the nature of a person when alone to turn to reflection on things, because he has no one with whom to converse, and there is nothing to occupy his hearing and sight. When this is so, he has no choice but to occupy his mind with thought. When he reflects on that state, his sight first falls upon the camel he is riding, and he sees a wondrous scene. If he looks upward, he sees nothing but the sky; if he looks right and left, he sees nothing but the mountains; if he looks downward, he sees nothing but the earth. It is as though God commanded him to look at a time of solitude and isolation from others, so that the impulse of pride and envy would not prevent him from looking. Then, in the time of solitude in the distant wilderness, he sees nothing other than these things, so God necessarily gathered them together in this verse.

The second: all created beings point to the Creator, but they are of two kinds. Some of them have both wisdom and desire in them together, and some have wisdom in them but no share of desire.

The first kind is like a person of beautiful face, gardens of delight, gold and silver and others. These things can be used as evidence for the Wise Creator, but they are objects of desire and sought by the soul. So God did not command reflection on them, because when one looks at them, there is a danger that the impulse of desire will overcome the impulse of wisdom, and that would prevent the completion of contemplation and reflection and cause the soul to be absorbed in love of them.

The second kind: this is like animals whose form has no beauty, but whose design carries profound wisdom, such as camels and others. Yet mentioning camels here is more fitting, because the Arabs are more accustomed to them. Likewise the sky, the mountains and the earth, for the signs of their origination and need are evident in them, and there is nothing in them that is a share of desire. Since this kind is such that the share of wisdom in it is complete, with safety from the crowding of desire, God therefore commanded reflection upon them. This is what presents itself to us at this point, and success is from God.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 88, verse 21–24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So remind; you are only one who reminds﴾

Know that when Exalted God had set out the proofs for the soundness of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) and the return (ma'ad), He said to His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿So remind; you are only one who reminds﴾. The reminding of the Messenger only takes place through mentioning these proofs and their like, urging reflection upon them, and warning against neglecting them. This is a command from Exalted God to the Messenger to remind and to be patient with every hindrance that accompanies it, and a clarification that he was sent for this purpose and no other. Therefore He said: ﴿you are only one who reminds﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾

The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿bi-musaytir﴾ means "one empowered over" (bi-musallat), like His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a compeller﴾ [Qaf: 45], and His saying: ﴿Will you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus: 99]. It has also been said that in the dialect of Tamim the ta' is vowelled with a fatha, since sayṭara is transitive in their usage. The meaning is that you were only commanded to remind; so you are not empowered over them to the extent that you would kill them, or compel them to faith. They said: then it was abrogated by the verse of fighting (naskh, abrogation). This is the view of all the exegetes. The discussion of the explanation of this word has already passed at His saying: ﴿Or are they the controllers?﴾ [At-Tur: 37].

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except one who turns away and disbelieves﴾ ﴿then God will punish him with the greatest punishment﴾

There are issues here.

First issue: In the verse there are two views.

One of them: it is a genuine exception (istithna' haqiqi). On this reckoning, from what is this exception made?

There are two possibilities:

The first: it is said the implied meaning is: "So remind, except the one who turns away and disbelieves."

The second: it is an exception from the pronoun in ﴿over them﴾, and the implied meaning is: "You are not over them a controller, except the one who turns away." It has been objected to this that he (peace be upon him) was not at that time commanded to fight. Its answer: perhaps the meaning is that you will become empowered only over the one who turns away.

The second view: it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati') from what precedes it, as you say in speech: "We sat discussing knowledge, except that many people do not desire it." Likewise here, the implied meaning is: "You are not accountable for them; but whoever of them turns away, God will punish him with the greatest punishment, which is the punishment of Hell." They said: the sign that the exception is disjunctive is the suitability of entering "anna" (that) into what follows the exception; when the exception is connected, that is not suitable. Do you not see that you say: "I have two hundred except a dirham," and "anna" cannot enter there, whereas here "anna" is suitable, for you say: "except that whoever turns away and disbelieves, God will punish him."

Second issue: It was read: "alā man tawallā" (with the particle of alerting), and in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "fa-innahu yu'adhdhibuhu" (then indeed He punishes him).

Third issue: He called it "the greatest punishment" for several reasons:

One: it has reached the limit of the punishment of disbelief, which is the greatest, because what is other than it, the punishment of wickedness (fisq), is below it. For this reason Exalted God said: ﴿We will surely make them taste the nearer punishment short of the greatest punishment﴾ [As-Sajdah: 21].

Second: it is the punishment in the lowest level of the Fire.

Third: the greatest punishment may occur in this world, namely by killing, the taking captive of offspring, and the seizure of wealth as spoils. The first view is more preferable and closer.
